patient.name: Sofia Marchetti
patient.complaint: Eight months of crampy lower abdominal pain, bloating and loose stools
background: Junior solicitor; long hours and exam stress
Bad gastroenteritis on holiday 10 months ago
No family history of bowel disease or coeliac disease

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young woman, recurrent pain relieved by defecation, bloating and altered habit, and normal tests; IBD, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer are the distractors and red flags exclude IBS.

points: Sofia, 27, eight months of **crampy lower abdominal pain**.
Pain **eases after she opens her bowels**.
Loose, urgent stools with mucus, 3 to 4 times a day; some days normal.
Bloated by evening; worse in busy weeks at work.

steps.lead: Recurrent pain, altered habit and bloating with nothing structural: a **functional** disorder. Sofia's loose stools make her **IBS-D**.
Sofia is a **woman** under **stress** whose symptoms began after **gastroenteritis**: three associations at once.
Cramps, loose stools, urgency, **mucus** and incomplete evacuation all fit. Her examination shows only **mild diffuse tenderness**.

visual.title: Where Sofia feels it
visual.caption: Diffuse, shifting lower abdominal cramps with no focal mass or guarding.

steps.lead: The key: Sofia's pain is **relieved by defecation**, the core of the **Rome criteria**.

steps.title: Rome IV in practice
nodes: At least 1 day a week, last 3 months
Or a change in stool frequency
Or a change in stool form
steps.caption: Pain plus at least two of the last three; onset at least 6 months ago.

steps.q: Which feature would make IBS unlikely in Sofia?
steps.r: **Weight loss** is a red flag. Bloating, mucus and pain eased by defecation all support IBS.

steps.lead: Sofia has none of the **red flags**: no bleeding, no weight loss, no systemic illness, no obstructive symptoms.
Sofia's work and confidence are suffering: **psychosocial morbidity** is the most important complication of IBS.

steps.text: Do not label an older patient with new symptoms, bleeding or weight loss as IBS. **Red flags mean it is not IBS.**

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' to rule out a differential: anti-TTG for coeliac, faecal calprotectin for IBD, CA125 in women; IBS itself is diagnosed clinically.

o: Clinical diagnosis with no red flags
steps.r: IBS is a **clinical** diagnosis: symptom criteria plus absent red flags and a normal basic screen.

steps.lead: Sofia's history meets the criteria; the tests are to **exclude** the differentials, not to prove IBS.

steps.title: Sofia's first-line bloods
steps.text: All normal: no anaemia, inflammation, thyroid disease or coeliac.

steps.lead: Sofia's normal **FBC, CRP/ESR, TFTs** and **anti-TTG** remove the common mimics. **CA125** is checked in women with IBS-like symptoms, especially older women.
Because Sofia's is **diarrhoea-predominant**, she also has a **faecal calprotectin**.

visual.title: Faecal calprotectin
visual.label: Sofia 22
visual.caption: Normal calprotectin: no mucosal inflammation, so IBD is unlikely.

steps.text: Calprotectin raised → think **IBD**. Anti-TTG positive → **coeliac**. Normal screen + Rome criteria + no red flags → **IBS**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': lifestyle and diet first, mebeverine for pain, then subtype-specific drugs (ispaghula for IBS-C, loperamide for IBS-D), then low-dose amitriptyline.

steps.lead: Sofia starts with **regular meals**, fluids, less caffeine and a trial of **low FODMAP**; **mebeverine** for the cramps.

steps.q: Sofia's cramps are her worst symptom. Which drug first?
steps.r: **Mebeverine** (antispasmodic) is first-line for pain and cramps. Loperamide is for diarrhoea; amitriptyline is second-line; avoid opioids.

steps.title: IBS treatment ladder
nodes: Lifestyle and diet (low FODMAP, soluble fibre)
By subtype: IBS-C ispaghula; IBS-D loperamide
steps.caption: Psychological therapy runs alongside at any stage.

steps.lead: Sofia takes **loperamide** before long court days. If symptoms persist, **low-dose amitriptyline** suits her diarrhoea-predominant IBS.

visual.title: Sofia's symptom severity (IBS-SSS)
visual.caption: Each step helps a little; most patients need a combination.

steps.text: **Amitriptyline** is better for **IBS-D** (it constipates); avoid it in IBS-C. **Lactulose** is avoided in IBS because it causes bloating.

steps.lead: Sofia's plan follows the **Rome criteria** for diagnosis and **NICE** IBS guidance with a dietitian-led **low FODMAP** diet.

steps.text: Do not reach for **opioid** painkillers in IBS: they worsen bloating and constipation and risk dependence.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: visceral hypersensitivity and gut-brain axis, why IBS follows gastroenteritis, how low FODMAP and TCAs work, and why calprotectin separates IBS from IBD.

steps.lead: Sofia's gut is not damaged; her **gut-brain axis** is turned up. Normal distension hurts because of **visceral hypersensitivity**, and stress makes it worse.

steps.title: Why Sofia hurts
nodes: Normal gas or stool distends the bowel
Pain eases when the bowel empties

steps.lead: Sofia's holiday **gastroenteritis** likely left low-grade **mucosal inflammation** and an altered **microbiota**: **post-infectious IBS**.

steps.q: Why does a low FODMAP diet help bloating?
o: Less fermentable carbohydrate reaches colonic bacteria
steps.r: **FODMAPs** are poorly absorbed, draw water in and are **fermented** by bacteria, producing gas. Cutting them reduces bloating and pain.

steps.lead: Mebeverine relaxes Sofia's **gut smooth muscle**; low FODMAP reduces fermentation; low-dose amitriptyline damps **pain perception**, not mood.
Sofia's calprotectin was normal because it comes from **neutrophils** in an inflamed mucosa, which IBS does not have.

prompts.q: What is IBS, what are its subtypes and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: functional, no structural disease.

points.p: Functional GI disorder: recurrent pain, altered bowel habit, bloating
IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M
Female sex, stress/anxiety, post-infectious, dietary triggers
points.why: Young woman is the classic stem.

prompts.q: How does IBS present and what is the key feature?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pain relieved by defecation.

points.p: Pain, bloating, change in bowel habit
Pain relieved by defecation (Rome criteria)
Examination: mild diffuse tenderness and bloating only

prompts.q: Which red flags mean it is not IBS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one red flag and the answer is not IBS.

points.p: Rectal bleeding
Weight loss
Severe systemic illness or obstructive symptoms

prompts.q: How do you distinguish IBS from IBD and coeliac disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match each mimic to its test.

points.p: IBD: bleeding, weight loss, raised CRP and calprotectin
Coeliac: positive anti-TTG
Most important IBS complication: psychosocial morbidity

prompts.q: Which first-line tests do you do in suspected IBS, and why each?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each test excludes a mimic.

points.p: FBC (anaemia, MCV for malabsorption)
ESR/CRP
TFTs
Anti-TTG
CA125 in women

prompts.q: How is IBS confirmed, and when is calprotectin used?

points.p: Clinical diagnosis: symptom criteria plus no red flags
Faecal calprotectin if diarrhoea-predominant or IBD suspected

prompts.q: What are the lifestyle, diet and first-line drug treatments?

points.p: Regular meals, fluids, less caffeine, review trigger foods
Low FODMAP diet; soluble fibre (ispaghula)
Mebeverine for pain; hyoscine butylbromide, peppermint oil

prompts.q: What do you give by subtype, and what if symptoms persist?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: C, D, then TCA.

points.p: IBS-C: ispaghula husk, macrogol option
IBS-D: loperamide
Refractory: low-dose amitriptyline (TCA), SSRI if not tolerated

prompts.q: What is the pathophysiology of IBS, and why can it follow infection?

points.p: Gut-brain axis dysregulation
Visceral hypersensitivity: low pain threshold to normal distension
Altered motility
Post-infectious: low-grade mucosal inflammation, altered microbiota

prompts.q: How do antispasmodics, low FODMAP, low-dose TCAs and calprotectin work?

points.p: Antispasmodics relax gut smooth muscle
Low FODMAP: less osmotic, fermentable carbohydrate
TCAs modulate visceral pain perception, independent of mood
Calprotectin: neutrophil protein raised by mucosal inflammation

glossary.IBS: Irritable bowel syndrome: a functional disorder of recurrent pain, bloating and altered bowel habit.
glossary.functional: Symptoms from abnormal gut function with no structural or biochemical disease.
glossary.IBS-M: IBS with mixed constipation and diarrhoea.
glossary.Rome criteria: Symptom-based diagnostic criteria for IBS centred on pain linked to defecation.
glossary.red flags: Features such as bleeding or weight loss that suggest serious disease and need investigation.
glossary.bloating: A feeling of abdominal fullness or swelling.
glossary.urgency: A sudden, hard-to-delay need to open the bowels.
glossary.incomplete evacuation: Feeling the bowel has not fully emptied after defecation.
glossary.post-infectious IBS: IBS that starts after an episode of gastroenteritis.
glossary.gut-brain axis: Two-way signalling between the gut and the brain via nerves, hormones and immune signals.
glossary.visceral hypersensitivity: A lowered pain threshold to normal stretching of the gut.
glossary.microbiota: The community of bacteria and other microbes living in the gut.
glossary.psychosocial morbidity: Psychological and social harm such as anxiety, depression and withdrawal.
glossary.CBT: Cognitive behavioural therapy: a talking therapy that changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviours.
glossary.gut-directed hypnotherapy: Hypnotherapy focused on reducing gut symptoms.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume; high or low suggests malabsorption of B12/folate or iron.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; a non-specific marker of inflammation.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; a marker of inflammation, normal in IBS.
glossary.anti-TTG: Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody; blood test for coeliac disease.
glossary.coeliac disease: Autoimmune reaction to gluten causing small bowel villous atrophy.
glossary.CA125: Tumour marker for ovarian cancer, checked in women with IBS-like symptoms.
glossary.faecal calprotectin: Neutrophil protein in stool; raised in IBD, normal in IBS.
glossary.IBD: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
glossary.low FODMAP: Diet low in fermentable oligo-, di- and monosaccharides and polyols.
glossary.FODMAP: Fermentable, poorly absorbed carbohydrates that draw in water and produce gas.
glossary.ispaghula husk: Soluble fibre bulking agent; first-line for IBS-C.
glossary.macrogol: Osmotic laxative, an option in IBS-C.
glossary.mebeverine: Antispasmodic that relaxes gut smooth muscle; first-line for IBS pain.
glossary.antispasmodic: A drug that relaxes gut smooth muscle to relieve cramps.
glossary.peppermint oil: Natural antispasmodic used for IBS cramps.
glossary.loperamide: Antimotility drug for diarrhoea; used occasionally in IBS-D.
glossary.amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for IBS pain.
glossary.SSRI: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; used in IBS if a TCA is not tolerated.
glossary.IBS-SSS: IBS Symptom Severity Score, out of 500.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has 1 year of recurrent lower abdominal cramps, bloating and loose stools with mucus. The pain improves after defecation. Symptoms are worse when she is stressed. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Examination shows mild diffuse tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Recurrent pain relieved by defecation with bloating, mucus and stress-related worsening, with normal bloods, is IBS.

steps.x: Diagnosis of chronic pain and altered habit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Older women, watery diarrhoea, often NSAIDs/PPIs.
Bloody diarrhoea and raised inflammatory markers.

steps.x: **B. Irritable bowel syndrome.** Normal tests + pain eased by defecation.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has 8 months of abdominal pain relieved by defecation and bloating. She opens her bowels every 3 to 4 days, passing hard pellets. She never has loose stools. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Bloods are normal.

steps.x: **D. IBS with constipation.** Hard only = C; loose only = D; both = M.
